Fiction/Non fiction?

If its a text book I think you are looking at it the wrong way. Having someone who has spent serious amount of time on a subject, is like meeting someone who has explored some part of jungle I haven't visited. The info that has accumulated in your head through that process is what is interesting.

I stopped reading books not because AI is mesmerizing but because I find the non-interactive nature of books irritating after too much AI use. ChatGPT allows me to stop and explore something, slow things down, bypass other things, connect it to other things etc etc

My suggestion would be make it interactive. Release it with an interactive interface rag or fine tuned to your ideas and content. Use your imagination on how that interactivity should be shaped.

text: I’m reverse engineering and replacing the entire stack on Samsung A54 (Exynos 1380, Mali-G68), started with booting to a customized linux kernel (7.3) w/o Android layer at all (Wayland and WPE WebKit only), built a custom WLBT thin firmware to replace the original fat blob (using mac80211 as the foundation), figured out how to exploit USB control transfer and got ACE in the PBL, reconstructed (with byte-identical verification) their LK-based S-Boot, uH and harx, patched mesa/panfrost, optimized kernels for this device (finally got STT/TTS running on GPU faster than on CPU), figured out how to utilize NPU, built a custom toolchain for it. I’m trying to properly own this device (and giving it to Claude on the lowest possible level, but still running pKVM and getting rid of original hypervisors), it’s the goal number one at this point, no binary blobs, ability to change sw and control hw on-the-fly. Obviously with AI usage (Opus 5.5/4.8, GLM 5.3, Kimi 3.1), there’s a lot of work.

Ages ago, I had built a tool to monitor the mains power frequency with resolution of some microseconds. I looked at my old assembly code, and realized with better optimization and optocoupler choice, I could probably get that down to some hundreds of nanoseconds.

The original idea was to try and correlate phase jitter to space weather, essentially using the mains power system as a sort of radio telescope. I never did get it working (although I did not have much time to try, either). I was able to see interesting things like generators spinning up to maintain the frequency though.

Will open source the hardware when done. I am not an astronomer, just some random fellow that investigates things at depth for no particular reason.

A suite of high-dopamine games which use smart exercise bikes as the control interface.

When playing Zwift, Rouvy, etc, I find that I get too competitive and ruin longer workouts by trying to keep up with or sprint past people who are much faster than me over long distances.

This is bad for building stamina and endurance, but I get bored, and it's hard to fight boredom and physical strain both at once.

I do not get bored sitting in front of Balatro, Raccoin, Tetris - anything with bright colours and satisfying noises and combos.

The first finished prototype game is very simple: you sort coloured marbles. Higher watt output from the bike means marbles are blown, by wind, upwards as they roll across the screen. Lower watt output means they fall. Steady watt output means they move horizontally. Marble goes into correct hole -> satisfying noise. It rewards steady watt output over time, with minor adjustments, which is what I'm trying to work on right now.

I was pretty amazed by how engaging I found it (total iPad baby brain). The miles really fly by - I get tired before I get bored.

I think that next I'll either do a tower defence game, or a less-dopamine-rewarding game in the style of Kerbal Space Program. Taking your actual weight and watt output, putting a bike with wings into a physics engine, and the gameplay loop being unlocking increasingly large airplane pieces, and designing - then flying - increasingly ridiculous airborne bicycles seems like a compelling idea, though less good for fitness.

The control surface being so limited - essentially one measurement which can either go up or down - is a really fun constraint for creativity.

I worked at a sports company forever ago, and ever since then, I've wanted to build my own NBA scores + stats site. After a few false starts over the years, I have a new concept called Center Court that I'm so excited about.

It's primary purpose is for live boxscores because all of the major sports sites have terrible UI/UX experiences. I always defaulted to ESPN.com but it's so slow and awful. Center Court is basically a bridge between espn.com (or nba.com) and more advanced stat focused sites that don't offer a good live experience.

The technical implementation behind it is quite novel in this space too. Instead of storing computed statistics in a database, I store raw play by play payloads immutability and everything else is derived from those and can be trivially rebuilt so the event log is a derived cache of the payloads. Every stat on every page is a pure fold over the event log at request time; no derived number is stored.

This enables some powerful features like being able to re-derive a game's entire state at any point of the game (or even a time range). Example game to try out: https://centercourtlive.com/game/0022600197 (https://centercourtlive.com/game/0022600197)

The site is meant to be extremely fast. It's all server-side rendered with progressive JS enhancements. URLs are immutable and cached behind a CDN.

https://centercourtlive.com/ (https://centercourtlive.com/)

Oh, C++.

C++ feels like an old lover who I think fondly of. We were together many years, until about C++20, through thick and thin. It was exhilarating - blazingly fast, perhaps irresponsibly so, but heck, the ride was wild. It taught me so many things, and shaped me into the programmer I am today. But we went our separate ways when its shortcomings became too large to bear, and its behavior - too often undefined - no longer excusable.

I keep up with it because I still have love for it, but I have to admit I am deeply concerned about many of the life choices it is making. I should have seen how problematic it was, because I knew its history, but I had hope that it could change, and it just looks like it never will.

I'm still rooting for C++, even though I am very happy with my new primary language, Rust. I hope it changes to the better, because I really want the best for it, but right now I'm just not seeing it. It keeps repeating old mistakes (e.g., more UB footguns with every new feature), without addressing any of the big flaws (insufficient tools for building robust software).

I sometimes still write C++, but I'm not excited about it the way I used to be. When I do write C++, it's because I have to. When given the choice, Rust is simply just a better choice for almost everything I do. Right now, I don't see a future for C++ and me.

I'm really torn about C++. I love C++ but there are things that I really don't like about it as well. It's a fantastic language in a lot of ways, but it carries around 40+ years of cruft, of things that you wouldn't do like that if you were inventing a programming language today.

I haven't written C++ professionally for many years at this point, and my memories of using it professionally (pre C++ 11) are not happy ones: having to agree on a strict subset of the language that we were allowed to use, which avoided features that any of the compilers didn't support well, or that my teammates didn't like. Sadly back then the list of forbidden features included templates and namespaces.

But using C++ on personal projects nowadays, and being able to choose which bits of the language to use - and which to avoid - is much more enjoyable. And honestly, the language did get a lot better from C++ 11 onwards.

I love C++, in the C++11 days I even organized a local C++ User Group at my university, and I've used it for the last 20 years as my main language.

I still appreciate its many merits but since a bit more than a year I migrated to Rust and I find it very difficult to look back, except for maintaining my previous C++ projects.

Surprisingly, it's not Rust's memory safety features that I miss the most when turning back to C++. It's mostly the absence of algebraic data types and pattern matching, and the split between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, i.e. concepts vs virtual classes, where in Rust you just have traits and use them for everything. On top of that the tooling and the ecosystem are just amazing.

There's a proposal for pattern matching sitting there under the committee's desk for some years now. With the mess that the standard committee is going through I really doubt they will be able to ship pattern matching for C++29 or even later. Too little too late.

So to answer the question, yes, I still appreciate the merits of C++ but I don't enjoy writing it as much as I have in the past.

Personally, I've never seen anyone write C++ codebases without boost. As you pointed out, the only practical way seems to be to constraint its feature complexity through meta programming.

Coming from the embedded C++ world where resources are scarce, C++ and its debugger ecosystem have been really nice. There were usually strong vendor provided SDKs and cross compilation toolchains available.

The issues I had with the language were mostly dependencies on vendors, not effectively being able to fix problems in SDKs, and as you also mentioned the footguns.

Lots of frustrations came from codestyle, branch conventions and type conventions we tried to encode into templates, which new team members had to learn before they could write any production code. So from a team perspective a lot of productivity came from reproducible build pipelines and setups. Having one team member on Windows and the other on macOS or Linux was as painful as it can get, especially with getting gcc's ecosystem to work properly. So you were also really dependent on Docker cross architecture images. And setting those up just for the sake of compilation was also unnecessary overhead.

These days I've migrated towards Go for pretty much all tasks I can think of, mostly for the tight integration with the C ABI ecosystem and tinygo and the easy possibility to cross compile into fat binaries.

What I miss though is a "real IDE" like the old Visual Studio, or geany or whatever. Most IDEs are not symbol based anymore, which makes them really painful to use in terms of what I expect an IDE to offer to be able to call itself an IDE. But maybe this is just my C++ heart bleeding all over the place because I miss good and typed API documentation examples that I can explore through clicking rather than having to google every function all the time.

I hope this is not a bad analogy but here goes.

Have you seen a Costco Food Court? The first time I saw it I thought of how inefficient it was. All these people crowded around a pickup window waiting for their number to be called.

They could easily build some sort of notification system so people would get a message on their phone when their order was ready. They could be shopping around the store rather than all waiting here.

Such an obvious opportunity for automation.

But after watching how they actually work and reflecting on it for a bit, I started to see why they don't do that.

- Letting people walk away likely means more orders will be piling up in their limited working space waiting to be picked up.

- These workers were fast. Juggling multiple orders at the same time. The "state" of the order is all in one place, a physical receipt and that state doesn't really change. Adding software to their workflow would almost certainly slow it all down (for reference, see hospital software).

- You'd have to train people on how to use the notification system. What happens when the system changes? What about security? What if someone were to hijack it and start sending out fake notifications?

My takeaway here is that every decision has trade-offs so before you think something can be automated you should understand what the manual process is first and why it works the way it does.

text:
A lot of it is general complexity. A lot of situations require not only complex behaviour that's quite tricky to program into a robot, but the ability to deal with situations outside of their control. Like on a production line, that's not an issue. There's no weather, there are no humans or other animals in the nearby environment, the parts all get transported at the same pace and in the same state, etc.

The robot can basically run a macro that goes from the same few motions over and over again.

Now think about a self-driving car. They're a lot closer to being practical now, but they still have a lot of challenges to deal with that the robot arms in factories don't.

They have to worry about legal issues if they make a mistake. There are other vehicles on the road, including both human driven ones and ones by other companies. There might be pedestrians nearby, or wildlife. Weather has an effect on how they drive, since even a machine can't react as well to flooded or icy roads as normal ones. There may be natural disasters, or ones caused by human/robot mistakes. The programming for this sort of system can't just follow a simple routine, it has to accounts for dozens or even hundreds of possibilities.

Same situation in many other places robots could be used in. Shops and restaurants, construction sites, on the street doing law enforcement and traffic work, etc. Unless you have an incredibly well-designed, incredibly flexible machine that can deal with unforeseen circumstances, it may be cheaper, easier and less legally risky to have a human do the work.

The easiest solution to this is to retool the layout of the space the robot will occupy to fit the needs of said robot. So, a shop or restaurant would be designed in a way that the automated setup would be closer to an oven or dishwasher and the process wouldn't interact with humans beyond the ordering and receiving aspects.

But that's expensive and time consuming to do, and in a lot of cases may hurt the business needs of the company. I don't think a lot of people want to get their food from the equivalent of a vending machine at a high-end restaurant, or have it delivered by a glorified roomba.

Unless humans become extremely expensive to hire and robotics becomes extremely cheap, that probably won't be worth the hassle to change.

text:
It's machine learning.

The process looks good for code and maths, but code has a fast feedback loop starting with "does it compile" and "do these unit tests pass?". It's OK to train models which start off with compiler errors 99.99% of the time and keep improving until it's >0.1% and it can just read and correct when those remaining errors happen.

Do that with a CNC milling machine, and it will drill through its own robotic arms a billion times before it gets good.

Remember: Tesla's fleet has about a trillion miles of real-world experience at this point, and yet the cybercab is extremely geofenced.

I know this isn't the answer you want, but I sell people on Signal based on the user features. I’ve had great success in getting my friends and family to adopt it.

Signal is incredible user friendly, privacy respecting, the gold standard for encryption, cross platform, etc. Yes, it’s centralized, yes it’s imperfect in many ways, but it’s easy and it’s pretty damn good.

If you want to help the people around you to become more involved in understanding and owning their tech, it has to be an easy and good experience. It has to be tangibly better, not just abstractly better with tangible downsides.

I use XMPP, but would never try to convince my friends and family to use it; it’s too complicated, the user facing apps all suck (Snikket and Cheogram are the best of the bad lot), and the incentives to use it aren't there. As you said, it’s just not attractive to a regular user, since it’s all around a worse experience than what they currently use. The one exception is that I do occasionally recommend XMPP for SIP access via jmp.chat to some of my more technical friends who have a tolerance for clunky user experiences in favor of privacy and affordability. I am holding onto an unreasonable hope that Signal or Whatsapp or others will consider XMPP+OMEO in the future to popularize the standard, but that is extremely unlikely.

Matrix also is an unfortunately terrible alternative to discord (even Element is a rather lacking user experience), so while I have pushed to move groups there before, I no longer recommend Matrix. I suggest signal or nextcloud as alternatives when possible; the remaining large groups who need the closed server forum style system are usually unlikely to move to Matrix anyway.

text:
My advice is not specific to Matrix but other self hosted private services.  Some of this may or may not be feasible with Matrix. (I have never used Matrix)

- Whether family or friends, always suggest it as a "fallback" for when "preferred service" is down and to use when discussion ultra-sensitive topics or sharing financial files.  With time they may just stay connected to it if the friction to do so is low.  It has to be their choice, not yours.

- What helps?  Add more incentives such as perks that "preferred service" does not offer.  No file size limits.  No or few file type limits.  No content filters.  Add emoji's or gifs that align with their inside jokes and their style of humor.  Keeping random people away is very important.  Making your friends and family administrators or moderators and let them decide how it operates.  Do not moderate or power-trip over your friends or family or they will leave.  Limit rules to "Do not break the laws of this country in public chatrooms" and private chat rooms if you do not physically host the server.   Database and file backups become even more important but they will feel in control of a thing.  Have a keyword or code word they all learn means to go check the private platform that "primary platform" would not recognize.  Maybe when they see "Turtle Farts!" they know to go log into your service.

- They may just stay on their primary preferred service.  Every group is different and not every group will see the benefits of your fallback service.  They may not appreciate the work you put into setting it up for them.  Do not expect to get the friends of your friends and family to move to your service.  They may not appreciate the OpSec value until "Bad Things"(c)™2038 happen to enough people.  Just be there for when it does.

- If there are concerns that you would spy on them, consider instead using eJapperd or Prosody as you can implement OMEMO for individual and group end-to-end encrypted messages.  Set up TLS fingerprint checks from multiple locations to reduce the risk of MitM attacks until XEP-0474: SASL SCRAM Downgrade Protection is fully supported and active by default on both servers and all clients.  This is the only thing holding me back from setting up a public Prosody server as 0474 is still experimental.  See [1]

- Avoid (block) federation on private servers for friends and family otherwise it is not a private server.

If you want to try it out you're always welcome to message me.

text:
I believe strongly in the mission of decentralizing the web, so I have relentlessly annoyed everyone into using matrix and/or Signal (not perfect but better). You have to set expectations that you won't convert everyone and that FOSS has warts. For that reason I bridge everything and always meet people where they are and constantly show off to them that even if they sms/telegram/WhatsApp/messenger/slack/discord/signal me then I get it in one app with no tracking or ads on my physical phone that I carry in my pocket. Many people in my social circle hate telegram but have to use it, so bridging that was a big selling point for example.

I also periodically take advantage of news stories that trend like when discord was going to ID people, I made a point to bring that up to convert more people, and always get a couple new takers.

When something fails to work like group messages fracturing or big files not sharing well with iPhone users, I make clear the practical value of having our own control and resources as a social network.

I also try to make sure my server has useful bots, a small thing but every bit of utility and differentiation with proprietary services helps.

I share guides on how to get back in, one thing people get confused about is that they don't have to give PII but they do need to remember the home server URL and save their key and password. So making sure to have ready pointers and blurbs on how to login that you can share quickly is necessary because people inevitably get logged out, especially iPhone users get confused easily (for app store culture reasons I think) and need kind but eager assistance.

I try to make sure we have well moderated safe space e2ee rooms to talk about hard issues, and people do realize over time that certain things are more awkward to say digitally if you know it could be being surveilled or tracked, even the metadata.

I've also encouraged technical friends to run their own servers and federate, got a couple to actually do it which is a cool feeling.

It takes time (years), patience, and effort, but many little pushes will build a community.

text:
Is your hypothesis that the lack of human imagination is preventing individuals from taking advantage of AI? Or that 'humanity as a whole' is not using it?

Just shooting some thoughts based on it, as its kind of fun:

Several things are needed for AI to be used by everyone, including not having a Butlerian Jihad. Because it is a threat to many's present ways of working, many do avoid it intentionally or have an aversion to it.

Reasonable or not, such fears certainly prevent people from taking advantage of it.

But at a level of 'humanity', the issue is mainly due to reality being physical. It takes movement of time, energy, and matter for things to change at those levels because of the fundamental physics that powers reality.

That and Government.

The bureaucracy governments have is like matter itself: heavy, difficult to move, and sometimes a burden, slowing things down as well. It can prevent overshooting as a dampening force, but it can certainly hinder progress (looking at you, EU).

Because Markets can represent the flow of time, energy, and matter, the structures and constraints they have put in place may themselves directly redirect assets to goods that don't produce functional value (leverage). This would be like the vast majority of NFTs and crypto-casinos, and perhaps physics-doomed technologies like Star Cloud. I digress...

AI, even SI existing for different companies, may be optimal for them, but the market may easily not be. It won't allocate resources more effectively.

Streamlined coordination between multiple companies enabled by SI, maybe. (Anthropic anyone?).

But in total, I would say the bottleneck is not Human Imagination. It is:

* Matter, Physics, Energy. 
* Governments
* Markets

text:
If you think AI is smarter than humans at "almost everything"...well, it might just be you.

On a side note, I really feel bad for Gen Z. Society has forced them to push AI as far as possible. They probably are the most aware of its limitations. Yet they are also the least able to criticize it without career repercussions.

I suspect this will change soon as more people come around to the fact that their chat bot is another tool just like Google search.

I used to think how wrong it was to compare an LLM to a search engine but have realized over time that despite being wrong, it's still a better mental model because it gets a fundamental detail right; LLMs are tools, they aren't agents, they aren't autonomous, they don't understand things, at least not in the way a human would understand them.

And this all ties back to the OP, that's the problem with calling them "smarter". Yes they can solve ancient math problems that humans failed at for many years and yet at the same time cannot be trusted to take a drive through order.

We need to stop seeing LLMs as a replacement for human cognition and instead appreciate what each form of "intelligence" brings to the table.

text:
Change the world how?

I was one of the very first users and developers of Bitcoin, April 2009 - Dec 2015. So for better or worse I did take part in something that changed the world. And here's the thing about that: you don't want lots of people changing the world. The world is as it is for reasons and many of the people who attempted to change the world ended up downgrading it, if not for themselves then for at least some other people. Textbook example: the long history of utopian socialist revolutions that always ended up bathed in blood.

There are relatively few world changes nowadays that everyone would agree on. That's why the utopian pitch for AI is always the same tiny handful of ideas, like curing cancer. Beyond basics like curing the last diseases, there aren't a whole lot of changes you can make that are obviously positive because most problems faced by modern societies are purely socio-political problems. They aren't problems that yield to application of intelligence. They're all about clashes of values and people struggling to impose their will on each other.

Of the few where it seems intelligence might make a difference, there are mundane reasons why it doesn't help much. Medicine is bottlenecked on clinical trials. They have far more ideas than they can check already, so generating even more won't help. Physics is bottlenecked on particle accelerator power. Ain't no LLM going to fix that. What might help is figuring out how those ideas would work out ahead of time, but that's hard because we can't simulate the body or the universe and LLMs don't have any magical solution to that either.

So the biggest impact of AI will continue to be in software, a domain where we actually are intelligence bottlenecked. LLMs can systematically drain the swampy backlogs of a gazillion badly maintained projects and that could probably absorb all the datacenter capacity being built today, if it were cheap enough. They can let us try out new platform architectures and then rewrite all the software that sits on top. Etc etc. And yeah right now some of that is limited by our imaginations and some of it is limited by cost, speed and other things that will hopefully continue to improve post-bubble.

I was visiting Ward Christensen on the day he got his first Toshiba laptop. After he got it powered up he realized that he had zero software on the 3 1/2" disks it used, making it almost useless.

It did have MS-DOS, thus it had debug. He used debug to write an impromptu assembly program to pull across data from one of his other machines via serial cable. He then used that code to pull across xmodem, which was then enough to pull across Qmodem. Then he pulled across laplink and he had rull access to everything.

It took less that 20 minutes total, I think.

I think it's interesting to interpret "Tears in the Rain" less broadly. The AI that we have today has much less than a four year "lifespan". It "expires" as soon as we stop typing into a session.

Interestingly, the best models can produce convincing poetry despite a lack of lived experience.

As realtime avatars and robots become more advanced, we will start to wonder more if somehow a system has some kind of consciousness, and then about real moral concerns. As technology practitioners, within a few years, our "tears in the rain" moments could come from actual interactions with AI.

But part of the point was about mortality being an aspect of nature to be accepted with grace. I think that's a practical reaction, and the typical attitude towards robots and mortality that a literature major or maybe just the average human would have.

But I believe that someone who really understands technology, and I would go so far as to say evolution (in the context of high technology), questions the optimality or at least necessity of natural death.

About 2 years ago, claude only had 200k(250k?) context; Even with clear instructions, the agents were not that disciplined; they usually suffered from attention deficit and they would start hallucinating in first 20 minutes. The subsystem that was being built had implementation plan, and a checkpoint file, which many agents didn't even bother to update frequently, so when a session occasionally crashed, it took a bit to resume the work. Most sessions would not last more then an hour or so.

One night, after a series of mediocre agents, a new session started, and the new agent started off by reading the plan, summarized the tasks ahead, and continued the implementation, frequently updated the checkpoints, and listed the status of tasks already done and pending.. this went on for the next 45 minutes and when the job was done the session ended. This was like a magic, seeing a master at work..

Since then I've wondered sometimes, if an enterprise grade llm (if there is such a thing) got misallocated to my task for that session.

text:
I was there, at the dawn of the Third Age of Mankind... (some called it the dot-com bubble)

I was a mere hobbit with my hobbit-computer pets, but I was holding the reins of something transcendent, untamed, and more colossal than I could imagine. My acquaintances discussing Free Software and stock trading and McMansion Purchases when their diploma ink was barely dry. Hiking through security doors and past Cray, Intel, DEC supercomputers and core routers -- quite the "wiring closet". The robots were safely imprisoned behind Plexiglas, and so were the console operators!

I gained enough skill and exhibited talent so as to fall into Silicon Valley, and Glenda deigned to ferry me back and forth, north and south, a one-man tornado wreaking havoc on the Information Superhighway. In the currents off Moffatt Field, and the shadow of Apple Computer's buildings I tried to rewrite network stacks but succumbed to Impostor Syndrome and its complications.

When California was done with me, Big Silicon and Oregon had use of my fingers + neural wetworks for awhile, and then I sprang at an opportunity to support astrobiology exploration and try to figure out an FC-AL SAN under a boss who didn't do Windows.

I had a third comeback. I graduated college. I had a good job and employer over 4 years. But sprinkled in all the family tumult and mental illness torments left me doubtful of what/whom I've been chasing. It was self-discovery, God-discovery, though: I also came to terms with adoption and meeting the strangers of my birth family: the inner life of an adoptee is itself unfathomable to outsiders. Just ask Harry Potter, Luke Skywalker, or Paddington Bear.

I'm scrounging for words now, but: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dreaming (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Dreaming) comes to mind, analogous to "Tears in the Rain" or Life Is But a Dream or, in the words of the indefatigable programmable roadside sign in L.A. Story:

  There are more things in Heaven and Earth, Horatio, than are dreamt of in your philosophy!

Roadside sign, I hug U!

text:
There are two ways I see to do this:

1. Tell your agent to eval the skill itself (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals)). This is easier and faster, but less accurate, and harder to extend to capture things like code quality.

2. Build your own benchmark out of work your normally do, and then eval the skill on that dataset. This is harder and more annoying (because creating benchmarks is hard) but provides deeper insight into how the skill affects the agent in known scenarios.

It also depends on what the skill is doing. If it's creating an artifact (like a report, easier to eval) then your strategy is very different than if the skill is changing agent behavior (like telling it to use cheap subagents under XYZ conditions, harder to eval).

The importance of doing this grows with the number of people using the skill. Working on my own projects, I don't usually bother. Working in an enterprise monorepo, suddenly the risk of shipping a bad skill is amplified, and evals become much more attractive.

Also note that skill behavior changes across different models. A skill built for Opus 4.8 may not be necessary on Opus 5.5. A skill built for Opus 5.5 might cause Haiku 5.5 to behave erratically.

TLDR: tell your agent to do it, and think about building your own.

A video player focussed on 360 videos.

I got a 360 camera (GoPro MAX v1) for my bicycle, after re-discovering bicycling during COVID. I soon found it was fun to review the video after a ride, but the software was a bit clunky. Upgraded to a DJI Osmo 360, and found the software likewise powerful, but still not what I wanted.

As an audio video developer I knew I could make it work the way I wanted, and this year I finally set about doing that:  https://recap360.app (https://recap360.app)  (macOS-only at the moment).

It’s a ~5MB download from the macOS app store; no in-app ads, no accounts, no ~GB download. It loads the video of a 5-hour bike ride in seconds, direct from MicroSD. Complete with a map overlay & graphs of various internal metadata.  (Speed, altitude, ascent rate, but also internal temperature etc).

It’s been fascinating to see the various tradeoffs the camera vendors make; how much in-camera stabilization & rolling shutter compensation vs how much to leave to the player.  Also interest ing is how the metadata is recorded in the file; some document them, most don’t.

Started with GoPro MAX, added DJI Osmo 360 & Insta360 support.  More coming soon.  Even plays dash cams & body cams (Vantrue & Boblov; I was curious to see how they stored GPS data).

text:
A new editor and processing engine for the Foveon Sensor cameras that were manufactured around 2002-2019.  The existing software is either wildly slow, or does not process according to manufacturer intention.  Think choosing between waiting multiple seconds after every single UI interaction to display changes, or color casts not being handled and the images looking green/magenta in different areas of the shot. One tricky bit is that the 4 different sensor architectures are all processed differently.

This weekend I am modifying the pipelines to be able to operate on downsampled sensor layers so that I can get multi shot editing as snappy as possible. Gave (https://gave.skar.cloud/en (https://gave.skar.cloud/en)) a wish list app for families available on iPhone and iPad.

"Gave" is Norwegian for "gift". It started as something I built for my family as each Christmas there were numerous bad solutions to making sure nobody knew what they got while still making sure that nobody got double up of something they wished for. I have iterated a lot over the last 3 years: I've built one version as a very simple web page, one version as a PWA, and now a fully-fledged native iOS and iPadOS app.

In Gave, the people who follow you can see what's free, reserved or bought, so nobody receives the same gift from two different people. You never see the status of your own wishes as the server never sends you that data. That goes for notifications, widgets, Siri and Spotlight too. There's a "Hide status" switch for when you show your screen to the person you're shopping for.

Some other things it does:

- Private notes and secret gift ideas.

- Easy view of whose birthdays and holidays are coming up, and if you are prepared.

- MCP server for connecting your favorite agent.

- Very native experience: It is integrated with Spotlight, Siri, deep linking, notifications and Apple Intelligence if you want to use it.

It's free: no ads, no subscription, no analytics, no affiliate links. Data lives on a server in Norway. Native SwiftUI on iOS 26, Laravel and Postgres on the backend. It now has English support as well, but the default language is Norwegian until the next version goes through review (hopefully today).

I'd love feedback, especially from anyone whose family has tried a shared spreadsheet or another wish list app and given up on it.

I started working on a tool to help us deal with the increased output from AI. Instead of reviewing large PRs, we review architecture diagrams with proofs. Most of the companies that my friends and I work at had stopped reviewing code, because it just became unmanageable. Also, working a 9 to 5, reading large outputs from LLMs got exhausting, even with the skills/plugins you throw in. The problem went beyond decision fatigue, I felt like I had a hard time understanding what the agent wanted to do or what it had just completed.

So I built https://draw.redcrayon.ai (https://draw.redcrayon.ai) (with a few friends), inspired by tools we love like Excalidraw: a live architecture board you and your coding agent draw on together. The agent connects over MCP (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, claude.ai) and draws what it changes as it works. The edges are meant to cite a source line (or fingerprint). You read the board instead of walls of text, and you can circle something in red crayon to get the agent to answer/fix it.

What we use it for:

- An incident scratch pad, where the agent lays out what it finds while debugging

- Seeing how a change affects the architecture before reading the diff

- Flagging the risky parts, like a DB migration, with every piece of code that reads that table

- Github App that generates a diagram per PR (something that is a work in progress)

- Ever wanted to create a branch of your existing diagram rather than completely clone/copy it? That's something we added to draw.

Docs: https://docs.redcrayon.ai (https://docs.redcrayon.ai)

OSS (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/redcrayonai/draw (https://github.com/redcrayonai/draw)

Relic AI: https://app.relic-app.com (https://app.relic-app.com)

Three of us in Sarajevo are building it.

It started because we kept saving things such as articles, Youtube lectures and podcasts, leaving open tabs as reminders for things to come back to later, but couldn't find those resources when we actually needed them, most of the time ending up redoing the research over again.

We have a browser extension for easy saving. It currently supports the page you're on, a PDF tab, all your open tabs, your bookmarks, and Youtube videos (including playlists). Each save gets a summary and tags. Then you can ask it questions, and it answers only from what you saved, with numbered sources. If nothing relevant is saved about what you are asking, it says so.

It's free during the beta and we are actively shipping new features based on user feedback.

I’d love to hear as much feedback as possible.

I’ve been building a little Python tool to extract a MIDI drum track from an mp3 or other song file.  Eventually I want to buy an e-drum kit and learn to play along with my favorite songs.

From what I can tell, we’re about even with the current state of the art in academic publications right now, at least on MDB.  Runs faster than real time in pytorch on a few years old MacBook.

It even does a decent job creating easy/medium/hard versions from the original “expert” track.  I compared ours to some charts from Rhythmverse and while we’re not as good as the official ones, we’re pretty darn close.

Spent some time trying to extract an instrument model for the drum sounds from the recording too, but I think that simply requires too much data for lots of the songs that I like where the mix is really dense with a ton of sound from distorted guitars and cymbals etc. Works a treat on super clean mixes like Back In Black though.

Next step is probably to create my own rhythm game, since my initial experience with Clone Hero and YARG left a lot to be desired.

As a heavy LLM user in my daily work, I've been working on optimizing agent memory on complex projects. That resulted in  this simple Rust-based tool called Wayfinder: https://github.com/zaterka/wayfinder (https://github.com/zaterka/wayfinder)

I've been trying to improve agent knowledge over a codebase, and existing approaches weren't giving the result I wanted, and I wanted to keep it simple. In the end, I added a semantic layer on top of an LLM Wiki and it saved 30% of token usage in multiple benchmarks I ran. It also adds some nice features to deal with concurring agents updating the shared memory, to ensure all information there is reliable and fresh.

It's published to PyPi, so an "uv tool install wayfinder-memory" already does all the work, and it's compatible with almost all Harnesses.

When I switched from C++ to C# many years ago because of a job, I felt a real ick. Not just because of garbage collection, I remember feeling repulsed by the fact that every class had a "ToString()" method! Bjarne says that the common denominator of all classes is the empty set! But also, an English word, made from letters! Yuck! Everyone knows that you should only ever overload operators because special characters are so much purer!

My C# days are now long gone as well, and I guess when I switched to JS/TS, I was so deep in the filth that I had just surrendered. I will say though, that looking back, I do feel like I was in a bit of a cult. I appreciate abstractions being free or near-free, but it feels like the language sort of wants you to engage in bike shedding.

text:
I have a love-hate relationship with C++. I am currently working with C++23 professionally in a complex project, with python layer on-top.

C++11 and later turned the scale more towards enjoyment, but having less time for tinkering and deep diving makes me annoyed. It's not entirely the core language's fault, but since high performance is the name of the game for C++, every library seems to make twists and turns to not leave anything on the table, which increases the cognitive load when writing code, be it performance critical or not.
AI now alleviates that quite a bit.

I wish it was as concise as python, e.g. with the list comprehension. When I try to use the newfangled ranges algorithms to replace a (range-based) for loop, I roll it back in 90% of the cases because it neither is shorter nor more expressive.

text:
when I didn't know better (i.e., didn't know many other languages), back in 96 to maybe 2002 or so, I tremendously enjoyed C++. I felt so powerful. It was hard to get things right and fast following the literature at the time, but hey, low-level, power, yay!

Then I took a turn and learnt LISP, ML, and a whole potpourri of functional languages. Things were so easy to express in comparison to looking at _all_ the details _all_ the time. I dropped my C++ for quite a while.

Fast forward a decade, and I spent about a decade writing C++11 code. Then C++17. I didn't particularly enjoy it, but it got the job done. In the environment at the time, alternatives were not accepted, so I obliged.

Now I just see loaded and unsecured footguns everywhere when I look at C++. Note that I'm still paid to write C++, but after learning to trust smart compilers in semantically proper languages, learned about data oriented programming, learned about all the bad from the pointer-laden object-oriented style, about the problems of (thread) synchronization C++ style vs. message passing between programs (CSP), ... I grew to despise it.

Frankly, nowadays, I'd rather write in Ada, drop all the "smart" constructs whose smell reek through the whole code-base, and all the implied semantics of various interfaces which are not described on language-level but (maybe, hopefully) in the comments ... the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink approach of C++ bites us regularly, but still, the environment has a hard time accepting non-C++ code.
